![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/c1b92084149ea54a3d309abf1a441c0f6855b15dc999f18c0108b02130d97ce8.png)

The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of a continuous function $y=f(x)$, is given above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there are two critical points: 

$\,$ $x=0\,$ and $\,x=1$ 

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,0)$ | $0$ | $(0,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $+$ | $\text{not def.}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical points. Consider the vertical lines $x=0$ and $x=1.$

- We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical line $x=0.$

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(0,1),$ the point at $x=1$ must be lower than the point at $x=0.$

So, we draw it as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/db3e0263e727e75197468f970ac85bdde2a2a9cdfb9257db0809665112772095.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(-\infty ,0)$ and increasing $↗$ on $(0,1)$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes down to the left and to the right of $x=0.$

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↗$ on $(0,1)$ and increasing $↗$ on $(1,\infty )$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes up to the left and to the right of $x=1.$

- Furthermore, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is constant to the left of $x=0$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ represents a section of a straight line on $(-\infty ,0).$ Also, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is increasing to the right of $x=0$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)>0.$ So, the curve $y=f(x)$ is concave up on $(0,\infty ).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/d8cf7b97d4e9356b275b669d59b0498286bc673d55fbc533891daac369d5cd35.png)

- Finally, since we are told that our graph must be continuous, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/5fc6864d1b7530ecd4fa1b151390b85d32a5d0628d0f51160cfaab7fc61e33b9.png)

**Note:** The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$
